title: Evidence of a possible turning point in solar UV-B over Canada, Europe and Japan
abstract: Abstract. This study examines the long-term variability of UV solar irradiances at 305 nm and 325 nm over selected sites in Canada, Europe and Japan. Site selection was restricted to the availability of the most complete UV spectroradiometric datasets during the period 1990–2011. The analysis includes the long-term variability of total ozone, aerosol optical depth and cloud fraction at the sites studied. The results, based on observations and modeling, suggest that over Canada, Europe and Japan the period under study can be divided into three sub-periods of scientific merit: the first period (1991–1994) is the period perturbed by the Pinatubo volcanic eruption, during which excess volcanic aerosol has enhanced the "conventional" amplification factor of UV-B at ground level by an additional factor that depends on solar elevation. The increase of the UV-B amplification factor is the result of enhanced scattering processes caused by the injection of huge amounts of volcanic aerosols during the perturbed period. The second period (1995–2006) is characterized by a 0.14% yr−1 increase in total ozone and an increasing trend in spectral irradiance by 0.94% yr−1 at 305 nm and 0.88% yr−1 at 325 nm. That paradox was caused by the significant decline of the aerosol optical depth by more than 1% yr−1 (the "brightening" effect) and the absence of any statistically significant trend in the cloud fraction. The third period (2007–2011) shows statistically significant evidence of a slowdown or even a turning point in the previously reported upward UV-B trends over Canada, Europe and Japan.
problem: This paper addresses the challenge of explaining long-term surface UV-B radiation trends, which are paradoxically affected by the opposing influences of ozone layer recovery (decreasing UV-B) and aerosol decline or "brightening" (increasing UV-B), to determine if the upward trend has finally reached a turning point.
method: This study analyzes long-term UV irradiance (1990-2011) from sites in Canada, Europe, and Japan using a statistical trend model and radiative transfer calculations to quantify the opposing effects of changing total ozone, aerosol optical depth, and cloud fraction on surface UV-B levels.
task: The task is to examine long-term solar UV-B irradiance trends over Canada, Europe, and Japan to identify a possible turning point, analyzing the influence of changes in total ozone, aerosol optical depth, and cloud fraction.
innovation: This paper presents evidence of a turning point around 2007 in the upward trend of solar UV-B radiation, showing that the effect of ozone recovery has recently started to dominate over the opposing "brightening" effect from declining aerosols in the Northern Hemisphere.

In addition to spectral UV solar irradiances and total ozone, this study includes the analysis of time series of aerosol optical depth (AOD) at 550nm and the cloud fraction from satellite data for the period 1990–2011. In the case of AOD, two overlapping datasets have been used: (1) for the period 1990-2006, the NASA/GACP, Global Aerosol Climatology Project (Mishchenko et al., 2007a); and (2) for the period 2000-2011, the Terra AOD experiment (MODIS) from the MODerate-resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (Levy et al., 2007).

In addition to spectral UV solar irradiances and total ozone, this study includes the analysis of time series of aerosol optical depth (AOD) at 550nm and the cloud fraction from satellite data for the period 1990–2011. In the case of AOD, two overlapping datasets have been used: (1) for the period 1990-2006, the NASA/GACP, Global Aerosol Climatology Project (Mishchenko et al., 2007a); and (2) for the period 2000-2011, the Terra AOD experiment (MODIS) from the MODerate-resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (Levy et al., 2007).

Similarly, cloud fraction data for the period 1990–2006 were taken from the NASA International Satellite Cloud Climatology Project (ISCCP), (Rossow and Schiffer, 1999) and for the period 2000–2011 the cloud fraction was taken from the MODIS/Terra dataset.

The procedure described by Reinsel (2002) and Newchurch et al. (2003), commonly used to investigate trends in ozone time series, was used in this work. We have applied here a statistical linear trend model, the generalized form of which can be described as the sum of a monthly trend, the QBO effect, the solar cycle effect, the cloud effect and a noise term as shown in Eq. (1): Yt =aTrt + β1Z1;t+β2Z2;t + β3Z3;t + Nt (1) where, Yt stands for the monthly deseasonalized UV data, Trt the monthly linear trend. Z1;t a proxy time series used to describe the QBO effect. Here we use 2 terms, namely the averaged equatorial zonal winds at 30 and 50 hPa. ... The statistical analysis using Eqs. (1) and (2) was applied to the time series of 305 nm and 325 nm, using the deseasonalised UV time series for the regions of Europe, Canada, Japan and their average.
